slides.title: Shell Index
items: An oyster-shell collection network
Illustrative seed pitch

slides.title: After the dinner rush
items: At closing time, shells from dozens of plates end up in a bin. Across the harbor, a nursery needs suitable material and a record of where it came from.
Shell Index coordinates the pickups, storage lots and signed transfers between them.

slides.title: A shell needs a record
items: LOT 042
North Quay / Tuesday pickup
A venue receives a lidded tote. The driver logs the source, pickup time and gross weight; the yard records empty-bin weight and a photograph.
Lots stay separate until a partner accepts the paperwork and its material checks.

slides.title: The receiving nursery signs
items: The nursery sets the receiving conditions. Shell Index records what passes inspection, what needs further holding and what must leave the restoration stream.
A signed transfer closes the lot. The originating restaurant receives a receipt for the accepted quantity.

slides.title: Follow a tonne through the yard
items: Collected shell mass after deducting bin tare.
920 kg
Eligible after sorting. The other 80 kg are logged as unsuitable for this lot.
900 kg
Accepted at transfer. A further 20 kg remain in holding pending review.

slides.title: Venues pay for collection
items: $160 / month
One scheduled weekly bin exchange, a pickup log and accepted-weight receipts. A missed or contaminated bin is documented on site.
$94 direct cost
Route labor and fuel account for $62, bins and washing for $18, and yard handling for $14. Contribution is $66 per venue-month.

slides.title: Density changes the route
items: Illustrative route labor and fuel per venue-month, dollars
A compact route spreads a shift over more stops. The pilot records actual drive time, bin-change time and kilograms accepted per venue.

slides.title: Start around one harbor
items: 80 venues
At $160 per month, eighty subscribing restaurants would produce $153,600 in annual collection revenue. Receiving-yard capacity limits the rollout.
First customers
Start with restaurant groups that can commit three nearby kitchens. Enroll a route only after a receiving partner signs off on expected volume.

slides.title: Why keep the lots separate?
items: General waste
Easy to arrange. The venue loses the recovery record when shells enter a mixed bin.
Volunteer runs
Valuable local capacity. Weekly continuity depends on people and storage being available.
Booked route
A named driver, a retained lot number and a receiving signature give both ends a record to reconcile.

slides.title: The people at each end
items: Iris Hart / collection
Iris designs the pickup runs and kitchen training. Her team can trace a disputed bin weight to the driver, time and original receipt.
Mara Quinn / receiving
Mara owns yard inspections and partner handovers. She holds a lot when the paperwork or condition falls short of the receiver’s requirements.

slides.title: A pilot with three gates
items: Pickup
Eight kitchens complete six consecutive weekly exchanges, each with a time and weight record.
Receiving
The yard reconciles every kilogram as held, rejected or transferred. A partner signs for each accepted lot.
Renewal
At least six kitchens renew at full price before the second route opens.

slides.title: Fund the first harbor route
items: $540k seed
$230k for bins and the receiving yard, $190k for collection staff and $120k for records and restaurant onboarding. The round funds a 15-month pilot.
Target: two signed receivers and 40 paying venues. Illustrative company and figures.
